subject: math
domain: Statistics and Probability — Making Inferences and Justifying Conclusions
cluster: Understand and evaluate random processes underlying statistical experiments

items.prompt: A school has $1{,}800$ students. A counselor surveys $150$ of them about lunch options. Identify the population and the sample in this study.
items.answer: Population: all $1{,}800$ students at the school. Sample: the $150$ students who were surveyed.

steps: The population is the entire group you want to learn about, which here is all $1{,}800$ students at the school.
The sample is the smaller group actually surveyed, which is the $150$ students.
So the population is all $1{,}800$ students and the sample is the $150$ surveyed students.

items.prompt: Classify each of the following as a parameter or a statistic: (a) the average height of all $400$ players in a basketball league, and (b) the average height of $30$ randomly chosen players from that league.
items.answer: (a) parameter (it describes the whole population of $400$ players); (b) statistic (it is computed from a sample of $30$ players).

steps: A parameter is a fixed number that describes an entire population; a statistic is a number computed from a sample.
(a) The average height of all $400$ players covers the whole population, so it is a parameter.
(b) The average height of $30$ randomly chosen players is computed from a sample, so it is a statistic.

items.prompt: A factory produces $50{,}000$ light bulbs in a day. A quality inspector randomly tests $200$ of them and records how many are defective. Identify the population and the sample.
items.answer: Population: all $50{,}000$ bulbs produced that day. Sample: the $200$ bulbs randomly tested.

steps: The population is the full group of interest: all $50{,}000$ bulbs produced that day.
The sample is the subset actually examined: the $200$ randomly tested bulbs.
Thus the population is the $50{,}000$ bulbs and the sample is the $200$ tested bulbs.

items.prompt: Match each quantity to its correct symbol from $\mu$, $p$, $\bar{x}$, $\hat{p}$: (a) the proportion of all registered voters who favor a measure; (b) the proportion of voters in a random sample who favor it; (c) the mean income of an entire city; (d) the mean income of a sample of households.

steps: Population values (parameters) use $\mu$ for a mean and $p$ for a proportion. Sample values (statistics) use $\bar{x}$ for a mean and $\hat{p}$ for a proportion.
(a) A proportion of all voters is a population proportion, so it is $p$.
(b) A proportion from a sample is a sample proportion, so it is $\hat{p}$.
(c) A mean of an entire city is a population mean, so it is $\mu$.
(d) A mean from a sample is a sample mean, so it is $\bar{x}$.

items.prompt: Across all $12{,}000$ employees of a company, exactly $64\%$ are satisfied with their benefits. In a random sample of $300$ employees, $61\%$ said they are satisfied. Which value is the parameter and which is the statistic? Write the symbol for each.
items.answer: $64\%$ is the parameter, written $p = 0.64$. $61\%$ is the statistic, written $\hat{p} = 0.61$.

steps: The $64\%$ describes all $12{,}000$ employees (the whole population), so it is the parameter $p = 0.64$.
The $61\%$ comes from the random sample of $300$ employees, so it is the statistic $\hat{p} = 0.61$.
Parameter: $p = 0.64$. Statistic: $\hat{p} = 0.61$.

items.prompt: A random sample of $40$ households finds a sample mean of $\bar{x} = 2.3$ pets per household. The researcher wants to estimate the mean number of pets per household, $\mu$, for the whole town. What is the best single (point) estimate of $\mu$, and which symbol estimates which?
items.answer: The best point estimate of $\mu$ is $\bar{x} = 2.3$ pets. The sample mean $\bar{x}$ estimates the population mean $\mu$.

steps: A sample statistic serves as a point estimate of the corresponding population parameter.
Here the sample mean $\bar{x} = 2.3$ estimates the unknown population mean $\mu$.
So the best single estimate of $\mu$ is $2.3$ pets per household, with $\bar{x}$ estimating $\mu$.

items.prompt: Two different random samples of $60$ adults each are asked how many hours they sleep. Sample 1 gives $\bar{x}_1 = 6.8$ hours and Sample 2 gives $\bar{x}_2 = 7.1$ hours. The true population mean is a single fixed number $\mu$. Explain why the two sample means differ.
items.answer: Each sample contains different randomly chosen people, so their means differ slightly. This is sampling variability: the statistic $\bar{x}$ changes from sample to sample while the parameter $\mu$ stays fixed.

steps: Random samples contain different individuals, so the numbers they produce will not be identical.
The population mean $\mu$ is one fixed value, but each sample mean $\bar{x}$ is computed from a different set of people, so $\bar{x}_1$ and $\bar{x}_2$ differ.
This expected difference from sample to sample is called sampling variability; it does not mean either sample is wrong.

items.prompt: A nutritionist randomly selects $250$ shoppers from a store's loyalty database and finds $\hat{p} = 0.36$ buy organic produce. Explain why drawing a random sample lets the nutritionist use $\hat{p}$ to estimate the population proportion $p$.
items.answer: Because each member of the population has a known, equal chance of being chosen, a random sample tends to resemble the whole population, so $\hat{p} = 0.36$ is a reasonable estimate of the population proportion $p$.

steps: Random selection gives every member of the population a known chance to be included, so no group is systematically left out.
This makes the sample representative of the population on average, so the sample proportion $\hat{p}$ tends to be close to the population proportion $p$.
Therefore the nutritionist can reasonably use $\hat{p} = 0.36$ as a point estimate of $p$.

items.prompt: Three independent random samples of $80$ voters report support proportions of $\hat{p}_1 = 0.54$, $\hat{p}_2 = 0.49$, and $\hat{p}_3 = 0.52$. A student claims that because the three values differ, at least two of the samples must contain mistakes. Is the student correct? Explain.
items.answer: No. The three values differ because of natural sampling variability, not mistakes. Each sample is a different set of voters, so $\hat{p}$ varies around the fixed population proportion $p$ even when every sample is collected correctly.

steps: Different random samples include different people, so their sample proportions $\hat{p}$ are expected to differ.
This variation around the single fixed parameter $p$ is sampling variability and is normal, not an error.
So the student is incorrect: the differing values are expected and do not indicate that any sample is wrong.

items.prompt: A teacher states: 'Since exactly $58\%$ of all students in the district passed the state exam, every random sample of $100$ students I take will show exactly $58\%$ passing.' Identify the error in this reasoning and correct it.
items.answer: The error reverses the role of variability: a sample statistic need not equal the parameter. Each random sample of $100$ will give a sample proportion $\hat{p}$ that is close to $p = 0.58$ but will vary from sample to sample, rarely landing on exactly $58\%$.

steps: The population proportion is fixed at $p = 0.58$, but a sample proportion $\hat{p}$ is computed from only $100$ students.
Because of sampling variability, $\hat{p}$ will differ from sample to sample and usually will not equal $0.58$ exactly.
The correct statement is that each sample's $\hat{p}$ will tend to be near $0.58$, not exactly equal to it.

items.prompt: A radio host invites listeners to call in and vote on a proposed tax; $71\%$ of the $1{,}100$ callers oppose it. The host concludes that about $71\%$ of all city residents oppose the tax. Name the type of bias present and explain why the conclusion is not justified.
items.answer: This is voluntary-response (self-selection) bias. People who call in choose themselves and tend to have strong opinions, so the callers are not representative of all residents. The large sample size does not fix this, so the inference to all residents is not justified.

steps: The callers chose to participate on their own, which makes this a voluntary-response sample.
Voluntary-response samples overrepresent people with strong feelings, so the $1{,}100$ callers are not representative of all city residents.
A larger sample does not remove this bias, so the host cannot validly conclude that $71\%$ of all residents oppose the tax.

items.prompt: To estimate the proportion of all county voters who support a measure, a worker surveys only voters leaving a single downtown coffee shop and reports $\hat{p} = 0.62$. Name the type of bias and explain why $\hat{p} = 0.62$ is not a trustworthy estimate of the population proportion $p$.
items.answer: This is convenience-sampling bias (a form of undercoverage). Coffee-shop customers are not representative of all county voters, so $\hat{p} = 0.62$ is biased and cannot be trusted as an estimate of $p$.

steps: The worker surveyed whoever was easy to reach at one location, which is a convenience sample.
Voters at a single downtown coffee shop differ systematically from the whole county (location, income, schedule), so many voter groups are undercovered.
Because the sample is not representative, $\hat{p} = 0.62$ is biased and is not a trustworthy estimate of the population proportion $p$.

items.prompt: A researcher randomly selects $200$ households from a complete city directory and finds $\hat{p} = 0.34$ own a pet. Is it reasonable to infer that about $34\%$ of all households in the city own a pet? Justify your answer in terms of the sampling method.
items.answer: Yes. Because the $200$ households were selected randomly from a complete list of all city households, the sample is representative, so $\hat{p} = 0.34$ is a justified estimate of the population proportion $p$. The inference that about $34\%$ of all households own a pet is reasonable.

steps: Random selection from a complete city directory gives every household a known chance of being chosen, so no group is systematically excluded.
This makes the sample of $200$ representative of all city households, so $\hat{p}$ should be close to the population proportion $p$.
Therefore inferring that about $34\%$ of all households own a pet is justified by the random sampling method.

items.prompt: Study A surveys $150$ randomly selected students from a college's full enrollment list and finds $\hat{p}_A = 0.40$ work part-time. Study B posts an online poll on the college website and the $600$ students who choose to respond give $\hat{p}_B = 0.55$. Which study supports a trustworthy inference about the proportion of all students who work part-time, and why?
items.answer: Study A. It uses a random sample from the full enrollment list, so it is representative and $\hat{p}_A = 0.40$ supports a valid inference. Study B is a voluntary-response sample, so despite its larger size it is biased and does not support a trustworthy inference.

steps: Study A randomly selects students from the complete enrollment list, giving every student a known chance to be chosen, so the sample is representative.
Study B relies on students who choose to respond to an online poll, which is voluntary response and overrepresents certain students.
A larger sample in Study B does not fix self-selection bias, so Study A is the one that supports a trustworthy inference about all students.

items.prompt: A city mails a satisfaction survey to $5{,}000$ randomly chosen residents, but only $450$ choose to mail it back, and of those $80\%$ report being satisfied. The city concludes that $80\%$ of all residents are satisfied. Identify the source of bias and explain why the conclusion may not be justified even though the residents were originally chosen at random.
items.answer: This is nonresponse bias. Even though the $5{,}000$ residents were chosen randomly, only $450$ responded, and those who chose to reply may differ systematically from non-responders. So the $80\%$ may not represent all residents, and the conclusion is not justified.

steps: The initial selection of $5{,}000$ residents was random, so selection itself was not biased.
However, only $450$ of them returned the survey, and the people who respond to mail surveys often differ from those who do not (nonresponse bias).
Because the responders may not represent all residents, the $80\%$ satisfaction figure cannot be safely generalized, so the city's conclusion is not justified.
